To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the planter class was not uniformly conservative in their attitudes toward the slaves, that they were not uniformly reactionary in their agricultural techniques, and that they were uniformly determined in their opposition to the British government.

the sugar planters in the British West Indian islands were a class of men who were not uniformly calloused toward their slaves, but who were, on the contrary, generally humane and considerate toward their slaves; who were not uniformly reactionary and unimaginative, but who were generally intelligent and resourceful men, and who were generally intelligent, resourceful and humane men.

the following questions. Did the sugar planters in the British Caribbean, before emancipation, display the characteristics attributed to them by the abolitionist historians? Did the planters, after emancipation, respond to the challenge posed by the abolition of slavery by abandoning the sugar industry?

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the West Indian planter class, which had been in a sense created by sugar production, and which was in turn dependent upon sugar, was not destroyed by emancipation.
the planter class, as a class, did not exist.
the West Indies were not ruined, that they were not even seriously damaged, by the Emancipation Act of 1834.4 The West Indies, however, were in a state of decline before emancipation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, while the planters of the British West Indies were not uniformly conservative or backward, neither were they a progressive or dynamic group of men.
the sugar industry in Jamaica, as in the other British West Indian colonies, was a system of production in which the planters were the principal actors.
the planters of the British West Indies were a class of entrepreneurs who, despite the handicaps of the sugar industry, were able to achieve a remarkable degree of economic success.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the planters' efforts to maintain their sugar estates in the post-emancipation period were more successful than has been generally recognized.

the planters were more innovative and flexible than previously assumed and that they were able to adapt to the new circumstances of a free labor force and to the changes in the world economy which occurred after the end of slavery.
the British West Indian planter was not a static figure.
